questions.question: Differentiate between phonetics and phonology.
questions.solution_html:
• Phonetics – studies physical properties of speech sounds – articulation, transmission
  • and perception – concerns sound form. Phonology - analyses how sounds are
  • organised – function within a language – focus on patterns and rules – role of sounds
  • in communication.

questions.question: Differentiate between releasing and arresting consonants with examples.
questions.solution_html:
• Releasing consonants - occur at the beginning of syllables – movement from a
  • consonantal closure toward a more open articulation for the following vowel – release
  • into the nucleus of the syllable – involve an outward motion of airflow – pronounced
  • with greater clarity and force. Eg. /b/ in bat. Arresting consonants - occur at the end
  • of syllables – movement from open vowel position to a consonantal closure – arrest or
  • close off the syllable – involve reduced or incomplete articulation – may be subject to
  • neutralisation or weakening processes. Eg. /t/ of bat.
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025
questions.final_answer: neutralisation or weakening processes. Eg. /t/ of bat.

questions.question: How does assimilation operate in connected speech? Explain with examples.
questions.solution_html:
• Assimilation – a sound changes because of the sound that comes before or after it –
  • makes speech flow smoothly – mostly affects consonants. Can be Phonemic or
  • Allophonic. Phonemic – one sound is replaced by a completely different one,
  • changing the identity of the phoneme. Eg clean boots /kli:n bu:ts/ becomes /kli:m
  • bu:ts/ - /n/ becomes /m/ before the bilabial /b/ in /bu:ts/. Allophonic – basic sound
  • remains the same – pronunciation shifts slightly. Eg. /hæz tu:/ becomes /hæs tu:/ - /z/
  • becomes /s/ due to the influence of the voiceless /t/
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025
questions.final_answer: becomes /s/ due to the influence of the voiceless /t

questions.question: Differentiate between segmental and suprasegmental features of speech.
questions.solution_html:
• A chain of phonemes that form speech segments and consonant clusters are known as
  • segmental features. Certain aspects of speech such as stress, pitch and length affect how
  • sounds are perceived. These are called suprasegmentals or sound attributes. Segmental
  • features relate to individual vowels and consonants; suprasegmentals shape the rhythm,
  • melody and overall flow of speech. /
questions.source_exam: III Semester MGU-UGP-(Hons) 2024 Admission Regular(Special Examination) Examination July 2026
questions.final_answer: melody and overall flow of speech.

questions.question: Describe the use and structure of the vowel diagram in phonetic study.
questions.solution_html:
• A vowel diagram is a visual representation of the position of the tongue during the
  • articulation of vowel sounds. It is usually a trapezoid or quadrilateral representing the oral
  • cavity. The vertical axis represents the tongue height, while the horizontal axis represents
  • tongue advancement. A vowel diagram helps in understanding how vowels are produced and
  • how they differ from each other based on tongue position. /

questions.question: Describe the general features of approximants and list the four approximants in English.
questions.solution_html:
• Approximants are consonant sounds produced when the articulators come close to each
  • other but do not create enough narrowing to produce turbulent airflow (friction). They are all
  • voiced in English - produced with a narrow but incomplete closure of the vocal tract. No
  • friction or turbulent airflow is created during articulation. All English approximants are
  • voiced, meaning the vocal cords vibrate. Air flows smoothly through the mouth. They are
  • classified into central approximants (air passes over the centre of the tongue) and lateral
  • approximants (air passes around the sides of the tongue). Approximants are often divided
  • into: Semivowels (glides): /j/ and /w/Liquids: /r/ and /l/ /

questions.question: Discuss how the respiratory, phonatory and articulatory systems work together to produce human speech.
questions.solution_html:
• Speech – complex activity involving multiple systems of the human body. The
  • respiratory system– provides the necessary airflow – comprises lungs, diaphragm,
  • intercostals muscles and trachea. The phonatory system includes the larynx and the
  • vocal cords – modifies the airstream by the vibration of the vocal folds. The
  • articulatory system – comprises nose, tongue, lips, teeth, and roof of the mouth -
  • shapes airstream distinct speech sounds like vowels and consonants. These systems
  • work together to transform breath into meaningful spoken language.

questions.question: Define the Cardinal Vowel System and explain how the primary cardinal vowels differ from their secondary counterparts.
questions.solution_html:
• The Cardinal Vowel System, developed by Daniel Jones, is an internationally accepted
  • framework for describing vowel sounds. It consists of 16 reference vowels—8 primary and 8
  • secondary.Primary cardinal vowels -[ɛ] [ɛ] [ɑ] [ɔ] [o] [u Secondary cardinal vowels-
  • ]y] [ø] [œ] [ɶ] [ɒ] [ʌ] [ɤ] [ɯ] The primary vowels define the extreme positions of the tongue,
  • while the secondary vowels are formed by reversing the lip-rounding of their primary
  • counterparts. Together, they provide a comprehensive and universal system for describing
  • and comparing the vowels of all languages. /

Biju: The doctor says there’s a severe infection in my intestines. They may even have to operate. The antibiotics and the loneliness are really wearing me down. Arun: Don’t worry, I’m here for you. What about your family? Biju: They come, but not often. My father is tied up with work from morning till night. Amma drops in regularly, but she can’t stay for long. Arun: And your other friends? Biju: Yes, a few visit, but they also don’t stay long. At times I feel so lonely, afraid, and depressed. Arun: That’s natural, but don’t lose heart. I have three consecutive holidays coming up. I’ll be here every day with a friend of mine. The three of us can spend long hours together—chatting, playing cards, and listening to music. I’ll also bring my i Pod, so whenever you feel bored you can listen. You’ve always loved music, haven’t you? Biju: Yes, that would really cheer me up. Arun: (steps outside and speaks to doctor) Doctor, may I know how long Biju will need to stay here? I hope it isn’t too serious. Doctor: It’s an intestinal problem. We’re running tests. He will recover—don’t worry. Arun: But how long will it take, Doctor? Doctor: We can’t say for sure until the reports come. Arun: Thank you, Doctor. Please take good care of my friend. (to Biju) Don’t worry, yaar. I spoke to the doctor—he said it’s nothing very serious. Now cheer up, let’s play some cards.
